Where do you put the stress in a phrasal verb?
If the phrasal verb needs an object, or is not separable, then you stress the verb.

Example:
cheat on
He cheated on his exam. ("He cheated on" is not finished without the object exam.)
She passed out because it was too hot.
If the phrasal verb is separable, then the stress is on the particle (preposition).

Example:
talk over
I would pick up a map and talk over my ideas with the concierge.
I would pick up a map and talk my ideas over with the concierge.
It would never have dawned on me to go to Japantown at 5 a.m.
You may not come across those extra special places on your own.
Aunt Nelly pointed out a lot places I would have missed!
Checking out a place or activity that most tourists don't know about, is the best part of sightseeing.
When you say a long sentence in English, you break it into distinct parts, each with its own intonation. You use the rise and fall of your voice to show the listener when you are or are not finished.
You break long sentences into parts, called clauses. Each clause has its own subject and verb (and sometimes object).
You also pause or break when you see a comma. A comma can separate a word or phrase from the rest of the sentence, or show where a clause ends.

For example:
When I checked into a hotel, // I would pick up a map and talk over my ideas with the concierge// who was more than happy to help.
At the end of each clause, you use rising intonation to show the listener that the sentence is not finished.
When you give opinions, the lead in to the opinion or reply is separated with a comma.

For example:
In my opinion, that's the best way to find out what's worth doing.

images.text:
Vanessa: What did you do for entertainment while you were away? See movies? Go to clubs?
Sally: Well, movies in another language didn't interest me. When I checked into a hotel, I would pick up a map and talk over my ideas with the concierge who was more than happy to help. In my opinion, that's the best way to find out what's worth doing. The concierge never let me down.

Vanessa: I couldn't agree more. It's the locals who always know where to send you. Aunt Nelly pointed out a lot places I would have missed!
Sally: The way I look at it, you may not come across those extra special places that are worth the effort to get to on your own.
Vanessa: Exactly. It would never have dawned on me to go to Japantown at 5 a.m., but it was captivating!

Sally: Finding museums that were off the beaten track was fun too.
Vanessa: I'd say that checking out a place or activity that most tourists don't know about is the best part of sightseeing.
Sally: Absolutely. Boy, this brings back memories!
